title: pneuma
summary: The references portray the Spirit in distinct settings. Ezekiel 36 promises cleansing, a new heart, and God’s Spirit; John 14 records Jesus’ promise that the Spirit will remain with and teach the disciples; Acts 2 narrates the Spirit’s coming at Pentecost; Romans 8 connects life in the Spirit with adoption and hope. Together these texts link renewal, presence, communal witness, and new life without reducing the Spirit’s work to one function.
historical_context: The set includes prophetic speech, Jesus’ farewell teaching, the narrative of Pentecost, and Paul’s letter to Rome. The source records support these biblical settings but no separate history of the Greek term or external reconstruction.
canonical_context: Ezekiel’s promise of the Spirit accompanies cleansing and a new heart. John 14 emphasizes the Spirit’s presence and teaching; Acts narrates the Spirit’s coming to the gathered disciples; Romans describes life in the Spirit and adoption. The sequence shows related portrayals while preserving each writer’s point.
literary_context: Prophetic promise, farewell teaching, narrative, and letter argument give the passages different emphases. Ezekiel announces renewal, John records Jesus’ promise, Acts narrates an event, and Romans explains its implications for life and identity. Readers can trace a connection without treating the forms as interchangeable.
covenantal_significance: The references connect the Spirit with renewal, presence, witness, and belonging. Ezekiel foregrounds a new heart, John the Spirit’s teaching presence, Acts the gathered community, and Romans adoption and life. These are complementary roles, not a single exhaustive definition.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages about the Spirit’s work in prophetic hope, Jesus’ teaching, the early community, and Paul’s account of life with God. It shows how these portrayals relate while remaining distinct.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce pneuma to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
